oneLineAnswer: Ticagrelor is an antiplatelet tablet that lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke in some heart patients.
whatItIs: Ticagrelor is an antiplatelet medicine you take by mouth as a tablet. Antiplatelet means it makes platelets, the tiny cell pieces that clump together into clots, less likely to stick. It blocks a docking point on platelets called P2Y12, which is where a signal molecule named ADP normally attaches. Its chemical formula is C23H28F2N6O4S. It is sold under the brand name Brilinta and was first approved in the United States in 2011.
whatItDoes: It blocks P2Y12, so platelets clump together less and clots form less easily.
In large trials it lowered the combined risk of heart-related death, heart attack and stroke.
The label lists three groups it is for.
The first is people after acute coronary syndrome, which means sudden reduced blood flow to the heart.
The others are people with coronary artery disease and no past heart attack or stroke, and people after a small stroke or a warning stroke called a TIA.
howPeopleUseIt: The label describes using it together with low-dose aspirin.
One trial analysis found better results when daily aspirin stayed at 100 mg or less.
The same analysis suggested higher aspirin doses reduce how well ticagrelor works.
People on it are often told not to stop on their own, because stopping raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.
It has been studied in people who also have diabetes and coronary artery disease.
It is also used around procedures such as stent placement, where the label notes it lowers the risk of a clot in the stent.

commonSideEffects: Bleeding is the most common problem, and it was the most frequent side effect in the trials.
Shortness of breath, called dyspnea, is the other common one.
Different trials put dyspnea at about 14 to 21 in every 100 people taking ticagrelor.
It is usually mild and often settles while the medicine continues.
A small number of people find it bad enough to stop the medicine.
LiverTox also lists headache, nausea, diarrhea, low blood pressure and allergic reactions.
Blood uric acid can rise, and gout was reported more often than with aspirin alone.
A rash has been reported since the medicine came to market.
seriousSigns: The label carries a boxed warning: bleeding can be serious and sometimes fatal.
Bleeding that is heavy, will not stop, or shows up in vomit, stool or urine is a warning sign.
Bleeding inside the skull is the most serious kind.
In one stroke trial there were 21 bleeds inside the skull on ticagrelor, against 6 on placebo.
Slow heartbeats and heart block, a problem with the heart's electrical signals, have been reported.
A rare blood disorder called thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) has been reported, and it needs prompt treatment.
Allergic reactions can include swelling of the face, lips or throat, called angioedema.
Pauses in breathing during sleep, called central sleep apnea, have been reported.
A rare serious problem is rhabdomyolysis, where muscle tissue breaks down.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone who has had bleeding inside the skull.
Anyone who is bleeding now, for example from a stomach ulcer.
Anyone who has reacted to ticagrelor with swelling such as angioedema.
It is not started in people who need urgent coronary artery bypass surgery, a heart operation.
The label says it is not recommended for larger strokes, scored above 5 on the NIH Stroke Scale.
It is not recommended for people given clot-dissolving treatment for a stroke.
People with severe liver disease should avoid it.
It is not recommended while breastfeeding.
Strong CYP3A inhibitors and inducers should be avoided with it.

interactions: CYP3A is a family of liver enzymes that break medicines down.
Strong CYP3A inhibitors raise ticagrelor levels, which adds to breathlessness and bleeding risk.
Examples include ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin and ritonavir.
Strong CYP3A inducers lower ticagrelor levels and can make it work less well.
Examples include rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine and phenobarbital.
Opioid painkillers such as morphine slow the stomach and reduce how much ticagrelor is absorbed.
Ticagrelor raises blood levels of the statins simvastatin, lovastatin and rosuvastatin.
The label sets lower limits for those statin doses.
The label says digoxin levels should be monitored when ticagrelor is started or changed.
Ticagrelor can give a false negative result on a lab test for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
pregnancyAndChildren: Pregnancy information for ticagrelor comes only from case reports. Those have not shown a clear link to birth defects, miscarriage or harm to the mother. Animal studies at high doses did cause problems in the offspring. No one knows whether ticagrelor passes into human breast milk. Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking it. The label says its safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Nobody knows how bleeding risk and clot risk line up with the measured platelet inhibition.
There are no studies of ticagrelor in people with severe liver disease.
Rare side effects found after approval have no reliable frequency, because reporting is voluntary.
How often ticagrelor injures the liver is unclear; LiverTox rates it a possible rare cause.
One trial analysis found the benefit looked smaller in North America than elsewhere, and the reason is debated.
Pregnancy safety rests on case reports rather than controlled studies.
This record does not cover doses, how to reverse bleeding, or what happens if a dose is missed.

gaps: NCCIH does not cover this substance. https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/ticagrelor returned HTTP 404, so no NCCIH page is cited.

NCBI Bookshelf blocked four direct HTTP attempts at the LiverTox ticagrelor page with a browser check. The page was then loaded in the in-app browser at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548529/ and read there, and it is cited from that fetch.

DailyMed drugInfo pages build their label text with JavaScript, so the direct fetcher returned only an empty shell. Label text was read from the openFDA label API instead, which serves the same SPL content.
DailyMed spls.json returned titles and set ids only, with no label text.
The PubChem compound web page requires JavaScript, so PubChem's REST API was used for identity and description.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were deliberately not fetched because NLM states they are copyrighted ASHP content. Only MedlinePlus health topic pages were used.
No public-domain source described a reversal agent, a monitoring schedule for bleeding, or outcomes past the trial follow-up periods.
No public-domain source was found on how ticagrelor affects people who are pregnant beyond case-report data, or on long-term use beyond the labelled conditions.

A MedlinePlus health topic on antiplatelet drugs was not available at the guessed URL https://medlineplus.gov/antiplateletdrugs.html (HTTP 404); the coronary artery disease topic was used instead for context on the condition.
This record intentionally contains no dosing, no reversal instructions and no advice about what to do if a dose is missed.
summary: This record covers what ticagrelor is, how it lowers clot risk after acute coronary syndrome, heart attack or stroke, its bleeding, breathing and interaction risks, and what remains unknown about it.
